verdicts.trueWording: The story actually begins with the land, situating us physically and geographically.
verdicts.note: Raw page (curl, browser UA) and WebFetch both give the full post. Quote and both limbs verbatim in the tone/prose-style paragraph.

verdicts.trueWording: while Ged is important to the story, he is also treated with detachment and clear-sightedness
verdicts.note: Quote verbatim on the raw page. 'By the narration' is a light gloss: the page attributes the detachment to how the story/Le Guin treats Ged, not to a named narrator.

verdicts.trueWording: Le Guin also writes the story in a heightened and at the same time tightened prose style.
verdicts.note: Quote verbatim; the claim's characterisation of the register matches the sentence exactly.

verdicts.trueWording: But unlike Tolkien, her prose has the sense of not a single word being used unnecessarily.
verdicts.note: Quote verbatim, and the Tolkien contrast is explicit ('unlike Tolkien'). Page adds it is not meant as a dig at Tolkien.

verdicts.trueWording: It is characterised by clear syntax, precise word choice, natural emphasis, and unobtrusive grammar.
verdicts.note: Raw HTML fetched with browser UA (the first WebFetch returned only a summarizer digest, so it was refetched). Carey self-identifies as a copy-editor earlier in the post, and introduces the paragraph as one he wrote himself.

verdicts.trueWording: Strunk and White's Elements of Style, corrected and supplemented by Miller and Swift's Words and Women, are my road-atlas to English, and have never led me astray.
verdicts.note: Quote verbatim inside the footnote marked 'Note (1989)' appended to 'Dreams Must Explain Themselves' (1973). 'Corrected' is the page's 'corrected and supplemented'.

verdicts.trueWording: without the careless reader's even noticing
verdicts.note: The quotation is verbatim on the page, and Carey's copy is identified as the revised 1989 Women's Press edition. But the page never mentions a Pendragon edition, a 1973 text, or any variant reading: 'Pendragon' appears zero times and the only 1973 dates are essay composition dates. The edition-comparison is the verifier's, not the source's.
verdicts.unsupportedLimb: the 1973 Pendragon text's reading 'the careless readers even noticing' - no variant, no Pendragon edition, and no textual comparison appears on the page

verdicts.trueWording: Prose often has three or even four unstressed syllables between stressed ones.
verdicts.note: PDF downloaded (HTTP 200, 1.54 MB) and text-extracted with pypdf. Section 'Rhythm in Language: Stress', under 'Frequency'. Poetry limb also verbatim: 'often only one unstressed syllable between stressed ones, and seldom more than two'.

verdicts.trueWording: This is the only difference between prose and poetry that I have ever been certain of.
verdicts.note: Under 'Regularity'. The antecedent of 'This' is the preceding pair of sentences: prose 'scrupulously avoids any noticeable regularity or pattern of stresses', and acquiring noticeable meter makes it stop being prose. Absence-of-metrical-regularity limb supported.

verdicts.trueWording: There are two elements to stress-rhythm in prose: first, actual syllabic stresses; second, syntactical phrases or word groups... These groups are what I call 'bars.'
verdicts.note: Section 'Stress-Rhythms in Prose'. Le Guin frames it as a tentative proposal ('Tentatively, I propose'), matching the claim's 'proposes'.

verdicts.trueWording: syntactical phrases or word groups, following syntax, punctuation, sense, stress, and breath
verdicts.note: Verbatim in the same proposal sentence; the following sentence names those groups 'bars', so the claim's subject is right.

verdicts.trueWording: good prose does have a stress-rhythm, subtle and complex and changing though it may be
verdicts.note: Verbatim. The claim's 'however subtle and changing' compresses 'subtle and complex and changing though it may be'.

verdicts.trueWording: Dull prose, clunky narrative, hard-to-read textbook stuff, lacks the rhythm that catches and drives and moves the reader's body and mind and heart.
verdicts.note: Verbatim, immediately after the good-prose sentence. 'Moves the reader' is the page's own final verb in the series.

verdicts.trueWording: Judson Jerome... says that poetry averages 40 to 60 stresses per 100 syllables, while prose averages about 20 to 40. My samples of prose run higher than that.
verdicts.note: Both limbs verbatim: the 20-40 prose figure is attributed to Judson Jerome, 'Poetry: Premeditated Art', and the sentence follows the eight hundred-syllable samples.

verdicts.trueWording: Number of stresses, most to fewest: 'Three Bears,' Woolf: 48 / Tolkien: 47
verdicts.note: Verbatim in the comparison table the claim cites. Noted as a source-internal inconsistency, not a defect in the claim: the per-sample section for 'The Three Bears' earlier reports 'Stresses: 49', against the table's 48. Le Guin's own factoid list also says Woolf and 'The Three Bears' share a stress-count.
